title: Pollen Drift, Gene Flow and Isolation Limits

content.overview: Cannabis pollen is wind-dispersed and can travel far beyond a source field. Distance reduces deposition but does not create a universal zero-risk boundary; weather, source size, landscape and neighboring production all matter.

vocabulary.definition: Movement of genetic material among populations through pollen, seed or other reproductive exchange.
Pattern describing how airborne particles are deposited with distance from a source.
Separation used to reduce cross-pollination risk, not a guarantee of zero pollen arrival.

sections.title: Most pollen falls nearer the source, but the tail matters
sections.body: A 2024 US modeling study found steep decline in simulated deposition within the first few kilometers while small fractions could travel much farther, creating a long-tail risk.

sections.title: Weather changes dispersal
sections.body: Wind structure, daytime convection and seasonal conditions influence transport and deposition, so one fixed distance cannot represent every location or day.

sections.title: Breeding and sinsemilla goals change consequence
sections.body: Unexpected pollen can alter seed production and genetic identity. Risk planning should match the consequence for the crop and surrounding production.

workedExamples: A small nearby pollen source and a large distant field may not present equivalent risk because source strength differs.
An isolation distance used successfully one season does not prove zero risk under different wind conditions.
commonMistakes: Treating one distance as a guarantee.
Assuming pollen risk ends at property lines.
content.practicalApplication: Map known/suspected pollen sources, prevailing seasonal wind and crop consequence, then document isolation, monitoring and communication strategies without claiming zero risk.
content.summary: Pollen isolation is risk reduction under uncertainty, not a universal distance rule.
